title: Hubble view of green filament in galaxy NGC 5972
caption: The twisting gas filaments of NGC 5972, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
credit: NASA, ESA, W. Keel (University of Alabama, USA)

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: Twisting through the darkness like a disturbed double helix, the ionized gas around the galaxy NGC 5972 forms an unusual structure. The gas seems to reel through space as if shaken by some huge disturbance, possibly a merger with another galaxy.

These sweeping trails glow in H-alpha light and in light from doubly ionized oxygen, both usually expected where stars are born and die. They stretch far beyond the stars that make up the main body of the galaxy. They reach so far that when Hubble used the filter needed to see the gas, the full extent of the clouds did not fit within its field of view.

NGC 5972 also has an active galactic nucleus. A supermassive black hole sits at its center, and material in the disc swirling around it moves so violently that twin beams of plasma shoot out in opposite directions at close to the speed of light.

understand.summary: This image combines Hubble data from the Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3, using broad filters and narrow filters that isolate glowing hydrogen and oxygen gas. The colors assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: The narrow filters isolate the specific glow of hydrogen and oxygen gas, making faint filaments stand out that would be far too dim for the eye.

explore: Because such jets carry enormous amounts of energy, they are best imaged at radio wavelengths, where they can form structures that dwarf their host galaxies. ESA points to Cygnus A, imaged by the NRAO Very Large Array, as an example. There, the galaxy's nucleus looks tiny beside its vast jets and lobes.
alt: A galaxy surrounded by twisting filaments of glowing gas that extend far beyond its stars, some reaching the edge of the frame.
